nameStory: Spanish needles earned its name from its sharp, needle-like seeds that stick to clothing and fur with barbed tips. Despite the 'Spanish' in its name, this plant is actually native to the Americas and likely got this moniker from early European settlers who associated anything prickly or troublesome with foreign origins.
description: Spanish needles is a tall, branching annual plant that can reach 3-5 feet in height. It produces small, inconspicuous yellow flowers that lack the showy white petals typical of many daisy family members. The plant is most memorable for its deeply divided, feathery leaves and its notorious black seeds that grab onto anything that brushes past. It's a late-season bloomer that often goes unnoticed until its sticky seeds make their presence known.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Black, needle-like seeds about half an inch long with 2-4 barbed bristles at the tip that feel sharp and cling tenaciously to fabric, fur, and skin

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into narrow, toothed segments that feel soft and delicate, arranged oppositely on the stem and resembling tiny fern fronds

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow disc flowers without white petals, appearing in clusters at branch tips and easily overlooked among the foliage

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, much-branched plant with a somewhat sprawling appearance, often forming dense patches in disturbed areas

habitat: Spanish needles thrives in disturbed soils, vacant lots, roadsides, and garden edges throughout New England. It prefers sunny locations with rich, moist soil but tolerates a wide range of conditions. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy plants in areas where the ground has been recently disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic feathery leaves beginning to develop.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly, reaching full height and beginning to branch extensively, with early flowers appearing in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming and seed production occurs, with the notorious sticky seeds becoming the plant's most noticeable feature as they cling to passersby.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stems may persist with empty seed heads, though most evidence of the plant disappears until spring germination.

funFact: A single Spanish needles plant can produce over 6,000 seeds, and those barbed bristles are so effective that they've inspired biomimetic research for developing new types of fasteners and adhesives.
confusionNotes: Spanish needles is most easily confused with other beggarticks species, but its deeply divided, fern-like leaves set it apart from most relatives that have simple or three-parted leaves. Remember: if the leaves look like delicate green feathers and the seeds grab your socks, you've found Spanish needles.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - Spanish needles has no connection to Spain and is actually a native North American plant. The 'needles' refer to the seeds, not thorns or spines on the plant itself, which is completely harmless to touch except for those clingy seeds.
compareHints: Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments. Devil's beggarticks, the most common relative, has simple oval leaves, while three-parted beggarticks has leaves split into just three broad leaflets.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
